column2: At the sipping of water, at the time of the Vaishvadeva, in other oblations and when applying ash, one should remember with devotion and great reverence Narayana called Rama, son of Jamadagni.
At the time of taking holy water three times, one should remember Krishna, Rama and Vyasadeva in turn; and at the time of lifting the conch-water, always remember the form of Mukunda.
With every mouthful one should remember the one called Govinda, the pure food; at the time of taking each item of food, O lord of birds, one should rightly remember Achyuta.
At the time of eating vegetables and the like one should always remember Dhanvantari; and when enjoying food from others, one should rightly remember Vishnu as Panduranga.
When eating fresh butter one should rightly remember Krishna called Tandava; when eating curd-rice one should always remember the supreme ancient one, Gopala-Krishna.
Likewise, at the time of eating milk-rice one should rightly remember Hari as Shrinivasa; when eating food cooked in fine oil and ghee, one should remember Vyankatesha.
Grapes, jambu, bananas, mangoes, oranges and pomegranates — when enjoying fine plantains, coconuts and amla, one should remember the child Krishna.
At the time of drinking a fine beverage one should rightly remember Vishnu called Narasimha; at the time of drinking the nectar of the Ganga, remember Vishnu, the Ganga's father.

At the time of setting out one should remember Narayana, whose mount is Tarkshya, beyond qualities, of universal form; at the time of kissing one's sons and others, one should remember Krishna with the flute in hand.
At the time of intimacy with one's own wife, always remember Hari who sports with the gopis; at the time of chewing betel, always remember Hari as Vasudeva called Pradyumna.
At bedtime always remember Hari in Vishnu's form called Sankarshana; at the time of sleep remember Padmanabha, and at the time of stories Hari in the form of Vyasa.
At the time of singing remember the flute-song, and always say "Hari, Hari." At the time of plucking the holy tulasi, remember "Shri Rama, Rama."
At the time of plucking flowers and the like, rightly remember Hari called Kapila; in circumambulation always remember Hari dwelling in Garuda, O lord of birds.
At the time of bowing to Vishnu, God of gods, remember Vishnu reclining on Shesha; at the time of good counsel remember Narasimha, and always remember Narayana.
When the completion of rites is made, one should rightly remember Hari as Vasudeva. Rites performed in this way please Hari.
Performing these properly, Pushkara became dear to Hari.
From this, lord of birds, comes the rite that has been described. Whoever hears with faith the incomparable story of Pushkara will always be joyful in the dharma that pleases Hari.
Because of her very fierce ill conduct, that brahmin's wife was abandoned by him. She then said to the lord of the earth:

Through the ripening of the fruit of my own deeds I was separated from my great-souled husband; this night-roamer was only the instrument.
markandeypuran:67:35	The fault is not his, nor that of my great-souled husband; the fault is mine alone and no one else's, for one reaps one's own deeds.
markandeypuran:67:36	In another birth I caused someone's separation; that same has now come to me. What fault is there in this great-souled one?
The rakshasa said: "At your command I will bring her to her husband's house, O lord; whatever else is to be done, command it, O king."
The king said: "When this is done, night-roamer, you will have done everything for me; and you must come, hero, when I remember you at the time of need."
The brahmin said: "O lord of men, if she has been devoured by beasts in the forest, enough of her; why do you not take the hand of another? Yielding to anger, you have not protected dharma."
The king said: "My beloved has not been devoured by beasts; she is alive, and her conduct is unblemished. How can I do this?"
The brahmin said: "If your wife is alive and not unfaithful, why do you commit the sin of living without a wife?"

The king said: "Even if she were brought back, O brahmin, she is always hostile to me; she would bring sorrow, not happiness, for she has no friendship toward me. So make an effort for me, that she may be devoted to me."
The brahmin said: "For your happiness, the excellent sacrifice that brings help, performed by those who desire friendship — the Mitravinda — I will perform for her.
It creates love between husband and wife who do not love each other, and it is the supreme generator of affection, O lord of men; I will perform that sacrifice.
Wherever your fair-browed wife is, O king, let her be brought from there; she will come to feel the greatest love for you."
Markandeya said: Told this, the lord of the earth brought all the materials, and that best of brahmins performed the sacrifice.
He performed the sacrifice seven times, again and again, that best of brahmins, to win back the king's wife.
When the great sage judged that friendship toward her husband had been implanted in her, the brahmin said to the king:
Let her who is dear to you be brought to your side, best of men; enjoy pleasures with her and, honoured, perform sacrifices.
Markandeya said: Addressed thus by the brahmin, the king was amazed, and he remembered that mighty, truthful night-roamer.
Remembered by him, the rakshasa at once came to the king, bowed and said, "What shall I do?" O great sage.
When the king had explained in detail, he went to Patala, took the queen and returned.
Brought back, she then looked on her husband with great affection and said again and again with joy, "Be gracious."
Then the king eagerly embraced the proud lady and said, "My love, I am already pleased; why do you say so again?"
The queen said: "If your mind is inclined to favour me, O king, then I ask this of you; do it as my due."
The king said: "Tell me fearlessly whatever you wish from me; nothing is unattainable for you, timid one; I am at your command, and not otherwise."
The queen said: "For my sake that Naga cursed my friend, his daughter, saying, 'You will be dumb'; and she has become dumb.
If out of love for me you are able to find a remedy for her, to remove the obstruction of her speech, what have you not done for me?"
Markandeya said: Then the king asked that brahmin what rite there was for this, to remove her dumbness; and he said to the king:
The brahmin said: "O king, at your word I will perform the Sarasvati sacrifice; let your wife be freed from her debt by the restoring of her friend's speech."
Markandeya said: That best of brahmins performed the Sarasvati sacrifice for her sake and recited the Sarasvati hymns with concentration.
Then, when her speech had returned, Garga said to her in Rasatala, "Your friend's husband has done you this most difficult service."
Learning this, Nanda went swiftly to the city; then the serpent's daughter embraced her friend the queen,
and praising the king again and again with blessings, the Naga maiden, having taken a seat, spoke sweetly:

The service you have now done me, hero, has won my heart; hear what I say.
markandeypuran:69:31	A son of great valour will be born to you, O king; his wheel will be unobstructed on this earth.
markandeypuran:69:32	Knowing the truth of all treatises on worldly aims, devoted to the practice of dharma, wise, lord of a manvantara — he will be a Manu.
Markandeya said: Having given him this boon, the daughter of the Naga king embraced her friend and went to Patala, O sage.
As the king enjoyed himself there with her and protected his subjects, a long time passed.
Then a son was born to that great-souled king, lovely as the full-orbed moon on the night of the full moon.
When that great-souled one was born all the people rejoiced; the gods' drums sounded and a rain of flowers fell.
Seeing his lovely form and his future character, the sages who had gathered named him Auttama:
He is born in an excellent (uttama) line at an excellent time, with excellent limbs; so he will be Auttama.
Markandeya said: The son of Uttama, known by the name Auttama, became a Manu; hear from me his power, O Bhaguri.
Whoever always hears the whole story of Uttama and the birth of Auttama never falls into enmity.
For one who hears or reads it there will never be separation from beloved wives, sons or kinsmen.
Hear from me, O brahmin, as I tell of his manvantara: who was Indra then, and who were the gods and sages.

You are children, ignorant of the meaning of words; that is why I said this: when the father is absent, women choose a husband themselves;
markandeypuran:71:35	but while my father lives, how can I choose, best of sages? Or if I have offended, be gracious, lord; I bow at your feet.
As she, bowed down, lamented thus, "Be gracious, be gracious," O wise one, that bull among sages said:

My word, once spoken, is never otherwise. You will become a doe after dying, in this very forest, in this very birth.
markandeypuran:71:38	And while you are a doe, a mighty-armed one will enter your womb — Lola, son of the sage Siddhavirya, passionate one.
markandeypuran:71:39	When he has come into your womb you will remember your former birth; regaining memory, you will speak with a human voice.
Markandeya said: Told this, the king too felt great joy: "My son, conquering my enemies, will be a Manu on earth."
Then that doe bore him a son endowed with auspicious marks; and when he was born, all beings rejoiced,
and especially the king, at the birth of his mighty son; and the doe, released from the curse, reached the unsurpassed worlds.
Then all the sages gathered, best of sages, and, foreseeing his future prosperity, named the great-souled one:
He was born while his mother was in a tamasic birth, and when the world was covered by darkness (tamas); so he will be Tamasa.
Then that Tamasa, raised in the forest by his father, having gained understanding, said to his father, best of sages:
Who are you, father? How am I your son, and who is my mother? Why have you come here? Tell me the truth.
Markandeya said: Then the mighty-armed father, the lord of the earth, told his son all that had happened — his fall from his kingdom and the rest.
Having heard it all, he worshipped the Sun and obtained all the divine weapons, together with the means of withdrawing them.
Skilled in weapons, he conquered those enemies, brought them before his father, and at his permission released them, keeping to his own dharma.
His father too, having seen his son's face with joy, gave up his body and reached his own worlds, earned by austerity and sacrifice.
Having conquered the whole earth, that king called Tamasa became the Manu called Tamasa; hear of his manvantara:
the gods, their lord, the king of the gods, the sages, and the sons of that Manu who protected the earth.
The Satyas, and also the Sudhis, the Surupas and the Haris — these were the groups of gods there, twenty-seven in each, O sage.
Of great strength and valour, marked by a hundred sacrifices, Shikhi was the Indra, lord of those gods.
Jyotirdharma, Prithu, Kavya, Chaitra, Agni, Valaka and Pivara, O brahmin, were the seven sages.
Nara, Kshanti, Shanta, Danta, Janu, Jangha and others were the sons of Tamasa, kings of great strength.
Thus the Tamasa manvantara has been described, O brahmin; whoever reads or hears it is not oppressed by darkness.
Of great strength and valour, sweet of speech and devoted to dharma, a king named Durgama will be her husband.
Markandeya said: Then, O sage, in the course of a hunt, the wise King Durgama came to his hermitage —
born of the line of Priyavrata, of great strength and prowess, son of Vikramashila, born from Kalindi's womb.
Entering the hermitage and not seeing the sage, the king addressed that slender maiden as "Beloved" and asked:
The king said: "Where has the blessed bull among sages gone from this hermitage? I wish to pay him my respects; tell me, lovely one."
Markandeya said: The brahmin had gone to the fire-hall; hearing the king's words and his address "Beloved," he came out in haste.
The sage saw the great-souled King Durgama bearing the marks of royalty, bowed with courtesy before him.
Seeing him, he said to his disciple Gautama, "Gautama, quickly bring the guest-offering for this lord of the earth.
First, he is a king who has come after a long time; and especially he is my son-in-law, so I hold him worthy of the offering."
Markandeya said: Then the king wondered why he was called son-in-law, but did not understand it; he remained silent and accepted the offering.
When the king was seated and had received the offering, the great sage bade him welcome and said, "Is all well at your home,
in your treasury, army and allies, your servants and ministers, O king, and in yourself, mighty-armed one, in whom all is established?
And is your wife well, since she is here? I ask after her; I do not ask whether your other wives are well."
The king said: "By your grace nothing is amiss with me anywhere, O you of good vows. But I am curious: which wife of mine is here, O sage?"
The sage said: "Revati, most fortunate, the most beautiful in the three worlds, is your lovely wife; do you not know her, O king?"
The king said: "Subhadra, Shanta's daughter, Kaveri's daughter, lord, Surashtraja, Sujata, Kadamba, Varuthaja,
Vipatha and Nandini I know as my wives at home, O brahmin; I do not know Revati, blessed one. Who is she?"
The sage said: "This fair maiden whom you just now called 'Beloved' — have you forgotten, O king? She is your praiseworthy wife."
The king said: "I did say it, but my intent was not wicked, O sage; you should not be angry with us; I beg you."
The sage said: "You speak the truth, O king; your intent was not wicked. You said it, O king, prompted by Fire.
I asked Fire, O king, 'Who will be her husband?' and he said, 'You yourself, the bridegroom, who comes today.'
So accept the maiden I give you, O king. You addressed her as 'Beloved'; why do you hesitate?"
Markandeya said: Addressed thus, the king fell silent, and the sage prepared to perform her wedding rites.
As her father prepared for the wedding, O great sage, the maiden, with face bowed in modesty, said:
If you love me, father, and would show me favour, let my wedding be held under the constellation Revati.
The sage said: "The constellation Revati is not in conjunction with the moon, good girl; there are other constellations suitable for your wedding, fair-browed one."
The maiden said: "Father, without it the time seems fruitless to me; how can the wedding of one like me take place at a fruitless time?"
The sage said: "An ascetic famed as Ritavak grew angry with Revati, and in his anger he threw the constellation down.
And I have promised him, bright-eyed one, as your husband; if you do not want the wedding, we are in trouble."
The maiden said: "Father, did that sage Ritavak practise such austerity, and not you, my father? Am I the daughter of a brahmin in name only?"
The sage said: "You are not the daughter of a brahmin in name only, child, nor of one without austerity; you are the daughter of me, who am able to create other gods."
The maiden said: "If my father is an ascetic, why not set that constellation back in the sky and hold my wedding under it?"
The sage said: "So be it; blessings on you, good girl, be happy. For your sake I will set the constellation Revati back on the moon's path."
Markandeya said: Then by the power of his austerity the great sage set the constellation Revati back in conjunction with the moon as before, O best of brahmins.
Having duly performed his daughter's wedding with mantras, he was glad and said to his son-in-law:
Tell me, O king, what wedding gift shall I give you? I will give even what is hard to obtain; my austerity is unobstructed.
The king said: "I was born in the line of Svayambhuva Manu, O sage; by your grace I ask for a son who will rule a manvantara."
The sage said: "This desire of yours will be fulfilled; your son will be a Manu and enjoy the whole earth, O king, and he will know dharma."
Markandeya said: Taking her, the king went to his own city; from Revati was born a son, Raivata Manu,
endowed with all the dharmas of men, unconquered, knowing the meaning of all the scriptures, versed in the Vedas, learning and treatises.
Hear with full attention, O brahmin, as I tell of the gods, sages, king of the gods and kings of his manvantara.
The gods there were the Sumedhases and the Bhupatis, O brahmin, the Vaikunthas and the Amitabhas, fourteen in each group.
The lord of these four groups of gods was the Indra named Vibhu, marked by a hundred sacrifices.
Hiranyaloma, Vedashri, and Urdhvabahu, Vedabahu, Sudhama and the great sage Parjanya,
and the fortunate Vasishtha, master of the Vedas and Vedanta — these were the seven sages in the period of Raivata Manu.
Balabandhu of great valour, Suyashtavya, Satyaka and others were the sons of Raivata Manu.
The Manus up to Raivata whom I have described to you all rest on the line of Svayambhuva, except for Svarochisha Manu.
Whoever always hears or reads this excellent narrative is freed from all sins and attains the world he desires.

Just as these are affectionate toward me for their own sake, so you too, acting out of self-interest, appear to me.
markandeypuran:73:11	But the Jatahārini (child-stealer) cat seeks to enjoy me, while you seek to enjoy fruit from me gradually.
markandeypuran:73:12	You do not know who I am, nor have I done you any service; our acquaintance is not long — only five or seven days.
markandeypuran:73:13	Still you love me with tears and embrace me tightly, and call me 'dear one, child, good one' without deceit.
The mother said: "I do not embrace you out of love for the sake of any service, child; if this does not please you, then I am abandoned by you.
I give up whatever benefit might come to me from you." Having said this, she let him go and left the birth-chamber.
Then the child-stealer carried off that abandoned child, dull in outward faculties but pure in inner nature.
Having carried off that child, she placed him in the bed of the newly delivered wife of King Vikranta and took her son.
Taking him to another house, she took that family's child in turn, and the third she devoured — so the child-stealer went on in order.
Carrying off child after child, she pitilessly devours the third, and daily makes such exchanges between the other two.
King Vikranta then had performed for that son all the sacraments proper to a kshatriya,
and his father duly gave him the name Ananda; King Vikranta was filled with the greatest joy.
When he had been invested with the sacred thread, his teacher said to the boy, "First go to your mother and pay her your respects."
Hearing his teacher's words, he laughed and said, "Which mother am I to revere — the one who bore me or the one who raised me?"
The teacher said: "This is not your mother, fortunate one, but Rutha's daughter, the chief queen of Vikranta, named Haimini."
Ananda said: "This is the mother of Chaitra, who lives in the village of Vishala, son of the eminent brahmin Bodha; the one born of her is elsewhere, I say."
The teacher said: "Where are you from, Ananda? Tell me. And who is this Chaitra you speak of? A great difficulty appears; where were you born? What are you saying?"
Ananda said: "I was born in the house of a kshatriya king, O brahmin, of his wife Giribhadra; the child-stealer took me.
She left me here and took Haimini's son, carrying him to the house of Bodha, chief of brahmins,
and devoured the son of that brahmin Bodha. There Haimini's son was raised with the brahmin sacraments.
Here we have been given the sacraments by you, our teacher, fortunate one. I must obey your word — which one should I approach, teacher?"
The teacher said: "A very deep and great difficulty has arisen, child. I understand nothing; my mind whirls with confusion."
Ananda said: "What room is there for confusion here, when the world is so ordered? Whose son is who, O brahmin sage, and who is whose kinsman?
From birth, whoever becomes related to men — other relations, O brahmin, are ended by death.
Even for one born here, the relation he has with his kin goes away when the body perishes; such is the whole course of things.
So I say: for one living in worldly existence, who is not a kinsman, and who is a kinsman forever? Why is your mind confused?
I have gained two fathers in this very birth, and two mothers; what wonder, when a body arises from another?
So I will practise austerity; have Chaitra, the true son of this king, brought here from the village of Vishala."
Markandeya said: Then the king, amazed, with his wife and kin, turned away his attachment and allowed him to go to the forest.
He brought his son Chaitra and made him fit for the kingdom, honouring the brahmin who had raised him as a son.
And Ananda, still a boy, practised austerity in the great forest to destroy the karmas that obstruct liberation.
As he performed austerity, the god Prajapati said to him, "Why do you practise severe austerity, child? Tell me."
Ananda said: "Blessed one, I practise austerity desiring purification of myself, intent on destroying the karmas that bind me."
Brahma said: "One whose office is exhausted becomes fit for liberation, not one who still has karma. When your office of sattva is fulfilled, you will attain liberation.
You are to be the sixth Manu; go and do that. Enough of austerity; when that is done you will attain liberation."
Markandeya said: Told this by Brahma, the wise one said, "So be it," and turning toward that duty he ceased from austerity.
Turning him from austerity, Brahma called him Chakshusha; by that former name he became famous as Chakshusha Manu.
He married Vidarbha, daughter of King Ugra, and begot on her sons of famous valour.
Hear, O brahmin, of the gods, sages, Indra and sons in the period of that lord of the manvantara.
The gods there were called Apyas, and one group of eight of them were of famous deeds, eaters of oblations in sacrifice, O brahmin.
Of famous strength and valour, hard to look at in their halos of light, the second group of eight gods was called the Prasutas.
Likewise another group of eight gods was called the Bhavyas; and the fourth group of eight there was called the Yuthagas.
Others were called the Lekhas in that manvantara, O brahmin; the gods of the fifth group, so named, were eaters of nectar.
Having performed a hundred sacrifices, their lord was Manojava, counted as Indra, enjoyer of the shares of sacrifice.
Sumedha, Viraja, Havishman, Unnata, Madhu, Atinama and Sahishnu were the seven sages.
Uru, Puru, Shatadyumna and others of great strength, the sons of Chakshusha Manu, became kings of the earth.
Thus I have told you, O brahmin, the sixth manvantara, and the birth and conduct of the great-souled Chakshusha.
The Manu now reigning is named Vaivasvata; hear from me of the gods and others of his, the seventh period.
The wise man on earth who recounts or hears this period of Chakshusha obtains sons and the wealth of health and happiness.
Chhaya-Sanjna said: "Goddess, until I am seized by the hair and threatened with a curse I will do as you say; I will tell what happened only if a curse is being drawn upon me."
Told this, the goddess then went to her father's house and saw Tvashtr there, his sins cleansed by austerity.
Honoured with great respect by Vishvakarma, the blameless one stayed in her father's house for some time.
Then, when she had stayed not very long, her father praised his lovely daughter and spoke to her with love and great respect:

As I look at you, dear child, even very many days seem like half a moment; but dharma is being violated.
markandeypuran:74:19	A long stay among kinsmen does not bring women fame; what kinsmen hope for is that a woman should live in her husband's house.
markandeypuran:74:20	You are united with your husband, the Sun, lord of the three worlds; you should not stay long in your father's house, my daughter.
markandeypuran:74:21	So go to your husband's house; I am pleased and you have been honoured by me. You must come back to see me again, auspicious one.
Markandeya said: Told this by her father, she said, "So be it," O sage, and having honoured her father she went to the Northern Kurus.
Not wanting the sun's heat and afraid of his radiance, she practised austerity there in the form of a mare.
Thinking the second woman to be Sanjna, the lord of day begot on her two sons and a lovely daughter.
Chhaya-Sanjna was exceedingly loving toward her own children, but did not behave so toward Sanjna's daughter and two sons.
Day by day she showed partiality in fondling and in comforts; Manu bore it, but Yama did not bear it from her.
In anger he raised his foot to strike her; yet, being forbearing again, he did not let it fall on her body.
Then Chhaya-Sanjna, in anger, cursed Yama, O brahmin, her lips trembling a little and her tender hands shaking:
Since you threaten me, your father's wife, with your foot, disregarding propriety, this foot of yours shall fall to the ground this very day.
Markandeya said: Hearing the curse his mother had given, Yama, stricken with fear, went to his father, bowed down and said:
Yama said: "Father, this is a great wonder, never seen by anyone — that a mother casts aside affection and curses her son.
As Manu tells me, she is not truly my mother; even if sons are faulty, a mother does not become faulty."
Markandeya said: Hearing Yama's words, the blessed dispeller of darkness summoned Chhaya-Sanjna and asked her where [Sanjna] had gone.
She said, "I am Sanjna, Tvashtr's daughter, O Vibhavasu, your wife; these children were begotten on me by you."
When Vivasvat asked her many times and she would not tell, the Radiant One grew angry and made ready to curse her.
Then she told Vivasvat what had happened; learning the matter, the blessed one went to Tvashtr's abode.
Then Tvashtr worshipped with supreme devotion the Radiant One, worshipped by the three worlds, who had come to his house.
Asked about Sanjna, the maker of all told him, "She came here to my house; I sent her back to you."
The Maker of day, entering meditation, saw her in the form of a mare practising austerity among the Northern Kurus.
The Maker of day understood the aim of her austerity: "May my husband be of gentle form and pleasing appearance."
Let my radiance be pared down today, the Sun said to Vishvakarma, Sanjna's father, O brahmin.
Then Vishvakarma, placing the sun on his lathe as it turned for a year, pared down his radiance, while the gods praised him.

Salutations to you whose form is the sun, whose nature is light; salutations to you, Bhaskara, and to the maker of day;
markandeypuran:75:8	salutations to the cause of night and the maker of twilight and moonlight. You are all this, blessed one; as you whirl the world about,
markandeypuran:75:9	the whole cosmic egg with moving and unmoving things whirls, driven by you. Touched by your rays, all this becomes pure;
markandeypuran:75:10	the purity of water and the like is brought about by the touch of your rays. The dharma of oblations, gifts and the like does not bring benefit
markandeypuran:75:11	as long as this world is not joined with your rays. All the Rig verses are yours, and the Yajus formulas too,
markandeypuran:75:12	and all the Samans fall from your body. You are made of the Rig, O Lord of the world, you are made of the Yajus,
markandeypuran:75:13	and since you are made of the Saman, O Lord, you are made of the three Vedas. You alone are the form of Brahman, higher and lower,
markandeypuran:75:14	with form and without form, subtle and existing in gross form; made of the nimesha, the kashtha and the rest, the form of time whose nature is decay — be gracious, and of your own will reduce your radiance.
Markandeya said: Praised thus by the gods and the divine sages, the imperishable mass of radiance then released his own radiance.
From his radiance made of the Rig came the earth; from that made of the Yajus, the sky; and the Sun's heaven is made of the Saman.
From the fifteen portions of radiance that Tvashtr pared away, the great-souled Tvashtr himself made Sharva's trident,
Vishnu's discus, the very fearful spikes of the Vasus, Agni's spear and Kubera's palanquin;
and whatever fierce weapons belong to the other enemies of the asuras, and to the Yakshas and Vidyadharas, the maker of all made them.
Then the blessed Lord bears a sixteenth portion; that radiance was pared into fifteen parts by Vishvakarma.
Then the Sun, taking the form of a horse, went to the Northern Kurus, and saw Sanjna there in the form of a mare.
Seeing him approach and fearing he was another male, she faced him, intent on guarding her rear.
Then, as the two met there and joined at the nostrils, two sons, Nasatya and Dasra, came forth from the mare's mouth;
and at the end of the seed arose Revanta, with sword, shield and armour, mounted on a horse and furnished with arrows and quiver.
Then the Radiant One showed his incomparable true form, and she, beholding it, was filled with joy.
Bhaskara, the thief of waters, brought Sanjna, his loving wife, now in her own form, to his abode.
Then her first son became Vaivasvata Manu; and the second son, Yama, became Dharmadrishti because of the curse.
His father himself set an end to the curse: "Worms will take flesh from his foot and fall to the ground."
Since he had the vision of dharma and was equal toward friend and foe, the dispeller of darkness appointed him to the office of Yama.
The Yamuna was born as a river flowing through Kalinda; the Ashvins were made the physicians of the gods by their great-souled father.
Revanta too was appointed lord of the Guhyakas. Now hear from me the appointments of Chhaya-Sanjna's sons.
Chhaya-Sanjna's elder son was like the first Manu; so the Sun's son received the name Savarni.
He too will be a Manu when Bali is Indra. Shanaishchara was appointed by his father among the planets.
The third of them, the daughter named Tapati, obtained from King Samvarana a son, Kuru, a lord of men.
Now I will tell you of the seventh period, that of Vaivasvata Manu: his sons, the kings, the sages, the gods and the lord of the gods.
Markandeya said: Then the two together, O brahmin, approached that sage — the merchant named Samadhi and that best of kings.
Having exchanged proper and fitting courtesies with him, the merchant and the king sat down and began some conversation.
The king said: "Blessed one, I wish to ask you one thing; tell me. It pains my mind because it is not under my own control:
though I have lost my kingdom, I still feel possessiveness toward all the parts of the kingdom, like one who does not know, though I know better. What is this, best of sages?
And this man has been wronged by his sons and wife, cast out by his servants and abandoned by his own people, yet he still feels great affection for them.
So he and I are both deeply unhappy, our minds drawn by possessiveness toward objects whose faults we have seen.
How is this, fortunate one, that delusion comes even to us who know? This folly belongs to me and to him, blind to discrimination."
The sage said: "Every creature has knowledge within the range of the senses, fortunate one, and sense objects come to each in different ways.
Some creatures are blind by day, others blind by night, and some creatures see equally by day and night.
Men are indeed knowers, but not they alone, for all creatures — cattle, birds, beasts and the rest — are knowers.
The knowledge men have, beasts and birds have too; and what they have, men have; in other respects both are alike.
Though knowledge exists, see these birds, though themselves tormented by hunger, out of delusion eagerly dropping grain into the beaks of their young.
Men, O tiger among men, long for sons out of greed, hoping for a return; do you not see this?
Still, they are cast into the whirlpool of possessiveness, the pit of delusion, by the power of Mahamaya, who maintains worldly existence.
So there should be no wonder at this: the yogic sleep of the Lord of the world is Hari's Mahamaya, and by her the world is so deluded.
For that blessed Goddess Mahamaya forcibly draws the minds even of the wise and hands them over to delusion.
By her this whole universe, moving and unmoving, is created; and she, when pleased, becomes the boon-giver who grants men liberation.
She is the supreme knowledge, the eternal cause of liberation, and she is also the cause of the bondage of worldly existence; she is the sovereign over all lords."
The king said: "Blessed one, who is that goddess whom you call Mahamaya? How did she arise, and what is her work, O brahmin?
What is that goddess's nature, what is her form, and what is her origin — all this I wish to hear from you, best of the knowers of Brahman."
The sage said: "She is eternal, the embodiment of the world, and by her all this is pervaded; yet her manifestation is manifold — hear it from me.
When she appears for the accomplishment of the gods' purposes, then, though eternal, she is said in the world to have arisen.
When at the end of the kalpa, the world having become one ocean, the blessed Lord Vishnu spread out Shesha and entered yogic sleep,
then two terrible asuras, the famous Madhu and Kaitabha, born from the dirt of Vishnu's ears, set out to kill Brahma.
Brahma the Prajapati, seated on the lotus of Vishnu's navel, seeing those two fierce asuras and Janardana asleep,
with a one-pointed heart praised that Yoganidra, who had made her dwelling in Hari's eyes, so that Hari might awaken.
Brahma, the Lord, praised the sovereign of the universe, upholder of the world, cause of its preservation and dissolution, the blessed Nidra of Vishnu, of incomparable radiance:
'You are Svaha, you are Svadha, you are the Vashat cry, you are the soul of sound; you are the nectar; in the eternal imperishable syllable you abide as the threefold matra,
and as the eternal half-matra that cannot be specially uttered. You alone are Sandhya and Savitri; you, Goddess, are the supreme mother.
By you all this is upheld, by you this world is created; by you it is protected, Goddess, and you always consume it at the end.
In creation you are the form of creation, in protection the form of preservation, and at the end the form of dissolution of this world, O you who are the world.
You are the great knowledge, the great illusion, the great intelligence, the great memory, the great delusion, the great goddess, the great sovereign.
You are the Prakriti of all, bringing forth the three qualities; you are the dark night of time, the great night, and the terrible night of delusion.
You are Shri, you are the sovereign, you are modesty, you are intellect marked by understanding; you are shame, nourishment, contentment, peace and forbearance.
Terrible, you bear the sword and the trident, the mace and the discus, the conch, the bow, arrows, the sling and the iron club.
Gentle, more gentle than all gentle things, exceedingly beautiful; you are the highest beyond high and low, the supreme sovereign.
Whatever thing exists anywhere, real or unreal, O self of all — the power of all that is you; how then can you be praised?
By you even he who creates, protects and devours the world has been brought under sleep; who here is able to praise you?
Since Vishnu, I and Ishana have been made by you to take on bodies, who could be able to praise you?
Praised thus for your noble powers, O Goddess, delude these two invincible asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha;
let Achyuta, Lord of the world, be quickly awakened, and let him be roused to slay these two great asuras.'"
The sage said: "Praised thus there by the Creator, the tamasic Goddess, in order to awaken Vishnu and slay Madhu and Kaitabha,
came forth from his eyes, mouth, nose, arms, heart and chest, and stood in the sight of Brahma, whose birth is unmanifest.
Released by her, Janardana, Lord of the world, rose from his serpent-couch in the single ocean, and then he saw those two,
the evil-souled Madhu and Kaitabha, of exceeding valour and prowess, their eyes red with anger, bent on devouring Brahma.
Rising, the blessed Lord Hari fought them for five thousand years, his arms his only weapons.
They too, maddened by their great strength and deluded by Mahamaya, said to Keshava, 'Choose a boon from us.'
The Blessed Lord said: 'If you are pleased with me, let both of you now be slain by me. What need of any other boon here? This alone is my choice.'
The sage said: Thus deceived, and seeing the whole world turned to water, they said to the lotus-eyed Lord:
'Slay us where the earth is not flooded with water; we are pleased with your fighting, and you are a worthy death for us.'
The sage said: Saying 'So be it,' the Lord, bearer of conch, discus and mace, placed their heads on his thighs and cut them off with the discus.
Thus she arose, praised by Brahma himself; hear further, I will tell you of this Goddess's power."
Varuna gave her a conch and Agni a spear; the Wind god gave her a bow and two quivers full of arrows.
The ocean of milk gave a spotless necklace and a pair of garments that never grow old, a divine crest-jewel, earrings and bracelets,
a bright crescent moon, armlets on all her arms, two spotless anklets, an unsurpassed necklace, and jewelled rings on all her fingers.
Vishvakarma gave her a most spotless axe, weapons of many forms and impenetrable armour.
The ocean gave her a garland of unfading lotuses for her head and another for her breast, and a most beautiful lotus.
Himavat gave her a lion as her mount and various jewels; the lord of wealth gave a drinking cup ever full of wine.
And Shesha, lord of all serpents, who bears this earth, gave her a serpent-necklace adorned with great gems.
